items.title: Assessing the Use, Impact, and Perspectives of Generative Artificial Intelligence Among Health Consumers: A Cross-Sectional Survey in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Saudi Health consumers increasingly rely on generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) to access health information from a growing number of health-related resources. Little is known about the frequency and patterns of generative AI tool use for seeking health information among consumers, its reported impact, and health consumers’ perceptions of these tools. This study aims to investigate the use of and perspectives on generative AI tools among health consumers in Saudi Arabia (SA). It also aims to assess the impact of their use on health-seeking behaviours. Methods: An exploratory, cross-sectional, self-administered online survey was distributed to adults (≥18 years) residing in SA during two data collection rounds in 2026 (March–April and July–August). All adults who used generative AI tools to seek online health information in the past year were included. Bivariate and multivariate analyses were conducted to examine relationships among variables. Results: A total of 403 eligible health consumers (58% male) participated. Among respondents who had used generative AI for health purposes, approximately 49% reported using it more than five times per month. Younger age, higher income, and more frequent pre-use were associated with higher odds of frequent seeking health information behaviour. Headache, abdominal pain, and musculoskeletal pain were the most common claims. ChatGPT was the main platform (84%) used for seeking information. Age was significantly negatively associated with frequency, whereas income and pre-visit use were positively associated. The primary reasons for seeking health information via generative AI were quick information retrieval (71%), time saving (34%), and curiosity (30.5%). Conclusions: The high frequency of use suggests that generative AI can serve as a source of health information and may lead users to withhold health information from healthcare providers. It may influence subsequent health-seeking behaviours, such as requesting urgent care or postponing physician visits. These self-reported findings do not establish diagnostic accuracy, clinical effectiveness, or patient safety, and the clinical risk and appropriateness of self-management actions were not assessed. Many respondents reported concerns about inaccurate information, missed serious illness, and increased health anxiety.

items.title: Association of ambient artificial intelligence scribe availability with patient instruction documentation and readability in ambulatory care
items.abstract: Abstract Objective This retrospective cohort study evaluated the effect of an artificial intelligence (AI) scribe on patient instructions documentation in ambulatory internal medicine settings. Materials and Methods We analyzed 391 061 adult encounters at a single medical center from December 2023 to July 2025. A difference-in-differences analysis estimated the relationship of AI scribe availability with patient instructions documentation frequency. Mixed-effects logistic regression estimated the association between encounter-level AI scribe utilization and documentation, adjusted for patient, clinician, and encounter characteristics. Length and readability were compared across instructions created by AI alone, clinicians assisted by AI, and clinicians alone. Character-level edit distances between AI drafts and final documentation were calculated. Results AI scribe availability was associated with a 10.5 percentage-point increase in patient instructions documentation frequency (P = .018), and encounter-level AI use was associated with higher odds of documentation (aOR 4.32; 95% CI, 4.14-4.50). AI instructions were longer than clinician-authored content (median 1994 vs 482 characters) and scored higher on 3 text-complexity indices (all P < .001). Clinician editing of AI content increased length without meaningfully reducing complexity. AI drafts and final documentation differed substantially, with a median character-level edit distance of 39.7%. Discussion AI scribe availability was associated with increased patient instructions documentation. However, AI-generated instructions were longer and scored as more linguistically complex than clinician-authored instructions, and clinician editing did not close this gap. Conclusion Ambient AI scribes can improve availability but may increase complexity of patient instructions. Research into downstream effects including patient comprehension and satisfaction is warranted.

items.title: Athlete-AI: a multi-modal artificial intelligence framework for personalized athlete monitoring and injury risk forecasting
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) provides opportunities for computational athlete monitoring, adaptive training analysis, and injury-risk modelling. This study presents Athlete-AI, a multimodal AI framework that integrates wearable sensor data, human motion information, pose features, and literature-derived athlete variables into a unified computational architecture. The framework combines multimodal feature fusion, reinforcement learning for adaptive training simulation, and machine-learning-based injury-risk modelling. The evaluation was conducted using publicly available benchmark datasets, including PAMAP2, Human3.6 M, and Microsoft COCO, together with literature-derived parameters used to construct simulated athlete profiles, workload, fatigue, recovery, and injury-risk scenarios. The framework was evaluated through computational experiments and simulation-based athlete-monitoring scenarios to examine multimodal integration, injury-risk classification, and adaptive training behaviour. Repeated-run evaluation across five random seeds, probability-calibration analysis, component ablation, comparison with multimodal fusion baselines, and a leakage-controlled analysis of the dependence on label-defining variables were also performed. When the workload, fatigue, recovery, and biomechanical-risk variables used to define the simulated labels were removed from the predictors, the F1-score decreased from 86.6 to 72.8%. Negative-control analyses showed that the benchmark-derived features-only model produced performance comparable to the shuffled-label control. The results demonstrate the computational feasibility of integrating heterogeneous athlete data and evaluating adaptive training and injury-risk modelling within a unified simulation environment. The reported performance values represent preliminary computational results and do not constitute real-world, clinical, or prospective athlete validation. Therefore, the proposed framework should be regarded as a computational research framework that requires validation with longitudinal data from real athletes before practical or clinical deployment.

items.title: Atlas: Making Sense of Long Horizon Agent Trajectories
items.abstract: AI agents can now search literature, generate hypotheses, analyze datasets, and run experiments at a scale difficult for researchers to match. Yet scaling scientific execution does not automatically scale researchers' ability to make sense of what agents produce. When researchers return to a long-horizon run, they must evaluate work they did not monitor: what the agent produced, which decisions shaped those outputs, and whether those decisions served the research goal. We frame this post-run sensemaking as a representation problem across three linked levels: goal, decision, and artifact. From this framework we developed Atlas, an agentic workspace with a trajectory tree, which renders the run as a branching structure showing what the agent chose and set aside, and artifact projections over six representations. In a within-subjects study (N=14), participants reported higher decision transparency, artifact sensemaking, and goal connection with Atlas than with a standard baseline, together with substantially lower subjective workload.

items.abstract: This systematic literature review investigates the evolution of automated adversary emulation and autonomous penetration testing, from attack graphs and classical planning approaches to reinforcement learning and large language model (LLM) based autonomous agents. The review examines how these approaches model attacker objectives, represent target environments, select attack actions and evaluate performance. It also assesses empirical evidence concerning the validity and limitations of the Cyber Kill Chain and MITRE ATT&CK frameworks for representing adversary behaviour. The review will use structured academic searches, predefined eligibility criteria, transparent study selection, quality appraisal and comparative narrative synthesis. Reporting will be guided by PRISMA 2020 and PRISMA-S, with methodological consideration of established software-engineering systematic review guidance. items.title: Automating quantum circuit optimization with AI agents
items.abstract: Compiling quantum algorithms for real devices involves hard optimization problems that can decide whether an algorithm runs at scale. We present a general method for solving such problems with AI agents, with every result certified. It builds on autoresearch loops, in which agents iteratively improve programs against a fixed evaluator and which have recently improved quantum cryptanalysis circuits, and adds two elements: a frozen, exact verifier certifies every result, and this verifier, together with the challenge around it, is built by an agent that formulates the problem with a researcher and validates the verifier against a solved case, deliberately broken solutions and published results before any solution exists. The method applies to any optimization problem whose solutions can be verified exactly and efficiently. We apply it to three compilation problems in quantum simulation, namely fermion-to-qubit encoding, Hamiltonian layout and unitary synthesis. In each, the agents improved substantially on published or standard constructions, reducing the cost being optimized by up to 73% at the largest sizes tested and outperforming a state-of-the-art optimizer for fermion-to-qubit encodings. Every submission is a program accompanied by its agent's notes, so the ideas behind each improvement are recorded in human-readable form; later agents built on them, and we describe them here. These results open the way to automated, certified discovery across quantum circuit design and beyond.

items.title: Automation of quality audits in healthcare services through information systems: a scoping review
items.abstract: This protocol describes a scoping review aimed at mapping the scientific literature on computerized systems, with or without artificial intelligence (AI), that automate quality auditing processes in healthcare services. Quality auditing supports patient safety and the identification of nonconformities; however, it is often a manual process based on data extraction from medical records and checklists organized in spreadsheets, placing a substantial workload on Quality Departments. Computerized systems, such as audit software, dashboards, rule-based systems, robotic process automation (RPA), machine learning, and natural language processing, have the potential to reduce this workload, improve information traceability and the resolution of nonconformities, and support evidence-based decision-making. However, the available evidence on this topic is scattered and heterogeneous, and no previous or ongoing reviews addressing this subject have been identified. The review will follow the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and the PRISMA-ScR guidelines, with searches conducted in national and international databases and grey literature sources, without restrictions on language or publication year. Study selection and data extraction will be performed by two independent reviewers, and the results will be presented in tables, figures, and an evidence map, accompanied by a narrative synthesis. The analysis will seek to characterize the systems, the quality dimensions audited, the technologies employed, and the benefits, barriers, and limitations associated with their implementation. Thus, the review is expected to identify knowledge gaps and inform future research and technological development in this emerging field.

items.title: Autonomous AI-Driven Security Operations Centers (Autonomous SOC): Agentic Orchestration, Real-Time Incident Response, and Multi-Agent Defensive Playbooks
items.abstract: Abstract—Contemporary enterprise Security Operations Centers (SOCs) are on the brink of systemic collapse driven by three converging factors: exponential alert fatigue (>25,000 uninvestigated alerts daily per enterprise), acute global cybersecurity workforce shortages, and the emergence of automated, machine-speed cyber threats executing multi-stage Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) in sub-minute time horizons. Traditional Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response (SOAR) platforms rely on brittle, rigid, hard-coded linear playbooks that fail when adversaries deviate slightly from known MITRE ATT&CK patterns. The paradigm of the Autonomous AI-Driven SOC (Autonomous SOC) establishes a transformative architecture that replaces rigid rule engines with specialized collaborative Multi-Agent Systems (MAS) powered by fine-tuned Large Language Models (LLMs) and Graph Neural Networks (GNNs). In an Autonomous SOC, decentralized cognitive agents autonomously triage alerts, execute deep forensic graph correlation, synthesize non-linear incident playbooks, isolate compromised endpoints via zero-trust API invocations, and conduct automated counter-adversarial negotiations. However, deploying autonomous agentic execution in mission-critical defensive infrastructure exposes severe risks: catastrophic hallucination loops during remediation, prompt injection propagation across defensive pipelines, decision deadlock, and unauthorized disruption of legitimate enterprise operations. This paper presents an exhaustive, mathematically formal technical investigation and empirical benchmark of Autonomous SOC architectures. We formalize incident response as a decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP) under dynamic threat uncertainty, model consensus verification over cryptographic remediation DAGs, and establish a dual-tier human-on-the-loop (HOTL) safety gating mechanism. Furthermore, we construct an enterprise SOC evaluation testbed spanning 10,000 multi-stage attack scenarios across real-world enterprise topologies. Our empirical findings demonstrate that our multi-agent autonomous framework slashes Mean Time to Detect (MTTD) from 18.4 minutes to 4.2 seconds and Mean Time to Remediate (MTTR) from 42.6 minutes to 18.2 seconds (a 99.3% reduction) while preserving a 99.6% remediation accuracy against MITRE ATT&CK kill chains. Finally, we formulate open challenges in adversarial prompt-injection resilience, continuous defensive co-evolution, and liability attribution under international cyber law.

items.title: Awareness and outcomes in undergraduate community engagement learning
items.abstract: Abstract Engaging community in stakeholder processes is important to the future viability and benefit of society. Research suggests that situational awareness factors of problem‐solving and transferable skills are key processes needed for successful community engagement. This study examined undergraduate student situational awareness using problem‐solving capacity and level of transferable skills in combination with student academic performance outcomes to determine overall capacity for community engagement. The purpose of this research was to discern if there was a predictive effect between student situational awareness and the instructional outcomes of a community engagement course. A pre‐ and post‐test research design using an event‐contingent survey sampling approach was used to determine potential for community engagement. Results indicated that students that had cognitive components of situational awareness including perception, comprehension, and projection were also likely to have transferable skills including reflection (pre‐course M = 3.88 to post‐course M = 4.02) and communication skills (pre‐course M = 4.19 to post‐course M = 4.24). Results of this research provide key takeaways to enhance student learning in the context of problem‐solving within a community engagement context. Helping students develop capacities and to see themselves as engaged problem solvers can provide an important set of skills to future community engagement professionals.

items.title: Balancing Skills and Values: Harmonizing AI in International Higher Education for Training and Upbringing
items.abstract: This chapter explores the dual role of artificial intelligence (AI) in international higher education, highlighting its potential to integrate skill-based training with value-oriented development across various cultural contexts. By utilizing continuous surveys and interviews conducted with both local and international students and faculty members from Belarus, Uzbekistan, and China, this study explores the perceptions, adoption, and integration of AI tools within sustainability-focused curricula. The findings, presented as recommendations, aim to balance technological efficiency with a human-centered approach to education, by offering a framework for culturally sensitive AI integration which aligns with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Furthermore, the recommendations emphasize curriculum development, faculty training, and institutional policies to ensure that AI supports the dual mission of higher education. The chapter was prepared within the research project “Develop a concept for using artificial intelligence to ensure the quality of the educational process in a higher education institution.“

items.title: Behavioral feature-based relevance ranking for tourism-policy recommendation: A decision-support framework
items.abstract: This paper develops a decision support system that ranks tourism-subsidy programs for individuals according to their travel behavior. Current tourism promotion policies in Korea distribute benefits through first-come-first-served mechanisms that ignore differences in traveler preferences. We address this by constructing individual-specific, penalized behavioral features — a baseline travel-propensity term and a distance-sensitivity term — using Zero-Truncated Negative Binomial (ZT-NB) models, grouping travelers with machine-learning-based Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) clustering, and ranking policies for each traveler through an explicit eligibility filter followed by segment similarity, geographic distance, and Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT)-based semantic similarity for natural language processing. Using 2024 Korea Tourism Survey data (n=3616 multi-destination travelers), we identify seven exploratory traveler segments and assess their stability by resampling the full pipeline. In a revealed-preference leave-one-out evaluation, scoring destinations by individual-specific behavioral features improves Hit@10 over random and nearest-neighbor baselines, but does not exceed a coarse region-match heuristic or a homogeneous-data artifact control, and remains below a simple pooled distance coefficient; the pooled (sample-level) distance effect and the single largest segment are the components that survive these controls. We therefore frame the artificial-intelligence contribution as exploratory behavioral segmentation and relevance ranking rather than demonstrated individual-level personalization, and the engineering application as a decision-support prototype rather than a validated mechanism for increasing travel uptake.

items.title: BeiDou-Enabled Personal Rescue Equipment for Urban Disaster Response: Functions, Scenarios and Technical Constraints
items.abstract: Disasters in urban areas are increasingly becoming complicated and this has required resilient positioning, communication and situational-awareness technologies of emergency responders. In this review, the potential of BeiDou Navigation Satellite System (BDS)-based individual rescue equipment in responding to disasters in urban and constructed settings will be discussed. A structured literature review was conducted to study representative rescue devices, including smart helmets, intelligent life jackets and personal positioning terminals, based on their technical functions and uses in disasters. The review combines the current capabilities of BDS-based positioning, satellite short-message communication, sensing integration and emergency information support. The findings indicate that BDS-based rescue systems can be used to enhance responder localisation, emergency communication and operational coordination particularly in situations where the terrestrial communication infrastructure is damaged or unavailable. However, they are constrained by urban signal blockage, multipath and non-line-of-sight effects, indoor positioning, power consumption and system integration problems. It is possible to note that the primary benefit of BDS, when compared to other GNSS constellations, is not necessarily a more accurate positioning in all circumstances, but a set of competitive PNT services and satellite short-message communication service. It also needs to be enhanced regarding hybrid positioning, multi-sensor fusion, low-power device design and integration with smart-city and digital-twin emergency-management platforms. These advances are essential to transform BDS-enabled rescue devices from standalone tools into components of resilient urban emergency-response networks.

items.title: Benchmarks Are Surprisingly Compaction-Friendly
items.abstract: Long horizon agentic tasks are now pushing LLM agents past their context window. To continue the task, the agent scaffold has to free up the context window, a process known as context compaction. Compaction is generally lossy by design: agents can silently lose task constraints, instructions, or their reasoning behind earlier decisions. Although compaction is a standard component of coding agent scaffolds, it has not been studied systematically with frontier models on realistic, long horizon agentic tasks. Previous work evaluate smaller open weight models on toy or synthetic trajectories. We fix the agent scaffold (OpenCode), implement five compaction strategies inside it, and evaluate three frontier models on three long horizon benchmarks (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench). For the two 1M context models, the compaction threshold does not measurably affect the task performance, whereas GPT-5.3-Codex, the model with the smallest context window, performs worse at lower thresholds on PaperBench and, less clearly, on PostTrainBench. No compaction method outperforms default self-summarization, and methods that discard more content cost some models up to 20 points while leaving other models the same. Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build. We argue that current benchmarks are compaction-friendly: i.e., the objective is fixed and the agent's progress stays on disk, so most of what compaction discards can be recovered, except constraints that don't exist anywhere else.

items.title: Between Artifice and Enlightenment: Queer Critique, Insecurity, and the AI Large Language Model
items.abstract: Abstract Over several decades, machine learning systems—often described with the double metaphor “artificial intelligence”—have become indispensable computational tools in the flow and mediation of economic and social capital. These systems can, on the surface, appear to deepen the dialectic of enlightenment identified by Horkheimer and Adorno by enabling ever greater domination over natural systems and human agency. They therefore generate widespread concern that computational advances endanger the security and autonomy of human subjects, especially in the sphere of production and exchange. Contemporary social theory offers conceptual tools that go beyond received categories of domination and autonomy, however, to provide a reanalysis of machine learning systems and their implication in social dynamics and economic relations. This chapter focuses on the ways large language model (LLM) systems demonstrate complex affinities with theories of mimesis and simulacrum, and therefore how such systems and require a rethinking of performativity and artifice. Recent queer critique—in which reflection on computational systems and simulacra is proliferating—and contemporary social theory, when read together, thus reveal how rhetoric about LLMs demonstrates slippages between agency, performance, reproduction, representation, and meaning that must be unpacked historically and conceptually before metaphors of the “artificial” and “intelligence” can carry analytical weight in addressing today’s socioeconomic relations. Ultimately, this theoretical-conceptual reading highlights the stakes of the problem of truth in systems where artifice manifests both socially and computationally.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Beyond Better Ideas: How Human-AI Collaboration Shapes Scientific Ideas and Human Perceptions
items.abstract: As AI increasingly becomes a collaborator in scientific research, its impact may extend beyond improving ideas to reshaping how they are evaluated, attributed, and perceived by humans. Yet existing research has largely examined these dimensions in isolation. We present a unified empirical study of Human-AI scientific ideation, investigating two complementary perspectives: i) how AI collaboration shapes scientific ideas and their evaluation, and ii) how firsthand collaboration reshapes human perceptions of AI. Through a shared experimental setting involving Human-AI and Human-Human research teams, human and LLM evaluators, collaboration-provenance analysis, and participant surveys, we uncover several counterintuitive findings. First, AI collaboration shows no significant advantage in human-evaluated idea quality, while iterative revision consistently improves quality. Second, AI judges can approximate human scores yet disagree on idea rankings; notably, an AI judge favors AI-assisted proposals without a corresponding advantage in human evaluations. Third, collaboration provenance remains only partially detectable, revealing substantial overlap between Human-AI and Human-Human scientific outputs. Finally, firsthand AI collaboration is associated with greater perceived usefulness but smaller efficiency gains than expected, suggesting a nuanced recalibration of human expectations. Overall, our findings challenge the notion that AI's value in scientific ideation lies primarily in producing better ideas, revealing instead its broader influence on scientific creation, evaluation, attribution, and human perceptions.

items.title: Beyond Chemistry Knowledge: Embedding Pedagogical Content Knowledge through an AI-Augmented Retrosynthesis Program for Chemistry Education
items.abstract: Abstract Synthetic route planning is a core learning objective in university organic chemistry, yet a challenging one requiring the development of advanced problem-solving skills. Existing computational tools often propose routes beyond the intended curriculum, limiting their suitability as learning resources. In this work, we introduce Retro-Learn, an educational retrosynthesis platform that integrates a curriculum-aligned reaction template library with large language model interfaces. The platform incorporates selected aspects of pedagogical content knowledge by aligning available reactions with the scope and sequence of instruction. An agent skill and a web-based chatbot enable route generation and visualization through natural language interaction. Evaluation using cumulative chapter-specific template libraries showed how the addition of reaction knowledge enables new routes and shorter solutions. Blind assessments of undergraduate examination problems showed higher mean chemical correctness scores than those of database-derived routes and scores comparable to or higher than those of general-purpose language models. Student survey responses indicated a plurality preference for Retro-Learn over general-purpose tools as a synthesis-planning learning aid. These findings illustrate how curriculum-specific chemical informatics and language model interfaces can translate pedagogical considerations into computational support for organic chemistry learning.

items.title: Beyond Heuristics and Commercial Navigation: An AI-Augmented Decision-Support for Ambulance Travel Time Estimation
items.abstract: Accurate ambulance travel time estimation is critical for emergency medical dispatch, yet existing decision-support practices often rely on static lookup tables or simplified assumptions regarding how ambulance travel time differs from ordinary passenger-car travel. For instance, they assume ambulances simply travel a fixed percentage (e.g., 5%) faster than ordinary passenger cars. However, such assumptions are rarely validated using real ambulance operational data and may fail to capture the effects of trip priority, temporal context, and origin-destination. We address these limitations using historical ambulance trips from the Skåne region in Sweden. Our analysis reveals that ambulance travel times vary substantially by hour, day, and trip priority, and that commercial navigation systems fail to capture emergency-specific dynamics. We contribute a machine learning system to more accurately estimate ambulance travel time. To make the system interpretable, we explored SHapley Additive exPlanations and permutation importance techniques to ensure that our system captures operationally meaningful patterns.

items.title: Beyond Parallel Domains: An Asymmetric Ecological Framework for AI-Mediated EFL in Saudi Arabia
items.abstract: English language education in Saudi Arabia is undergoing transforming amid broader economic, educational, and technological reforms. English plays an important role in higher education, professional development, internationalization, and participation in the knowledge-based economy, while young Saudis increasingly engage with English through social media, entertainment, gaming, and digital communication. Generative AI is also reshaping how learners access, produce, practice, and evaluate language. However, Saudi EFL research often treats language policy, classroom practice, learner attitudes, and technology as separate domains, potentially obscuring their dynamic interactions. Drawing on language policy and planning, language ecology, human-capital perspectives, and sociocultural approaches, this conceptual article proposes the Saudi EFL Ecological Transformation Framework (SEETF). The framework conceptualizes Saudi EFL as a dynamic ecology shaped by three interacting forces: language policy, economic transformation, and youth language practices, with generative AI functioning as a cross-cutting mediating force that alters the speed, visibility, and form of these interactions. It emphasizes policy enactment, learner agency, informal language practices, and asymmetries in influence and in the pace of change across institutional and societal contexts. The article advances seven conceptual propositions and argues that the future of Saudi EFL depends not on expanding English instruction but on coordinating these forces across differing timescales and degrees of institutional control.

items.title: Beyond routine drills: the role of specialized disaster education in fostering disaster awareness and preparedness
items.abstract: Understanding how disaster education enhances awareness and preparedness is crucial for improving community resilience to disasters. Although Japan widely implements routine evacuation drills, these may not foster an autonomous understanding of hazard characteristics. Conversely, specialized disaster education—such as survivor talks or field activities—provides deeper engagement; however, empirical evidence of its association with later awareness and preparedness remains limited. This study examined whether specialized disaster education correlates with higher disaster awareness and preparedness among young adults in Japan compared to standard evacuation drills. A nationwide online questionnaire survey obtained valid responses from 1,479 participants in their twenties. Respondents were divided into Specialized Education and Standard Drill groups, and their awareness and preparedness behaviors were analyzed using descriptive statistics and ordinal logistic regression with partial proportional-odds models. The results showed that the Specialized Education group had significantly higher awareness of local disaster risks and greater preparedness than those in the Standard Drill group, who were often neutral or undecided. Among the key indicators, the positive impact of specialized disaster education surpassed that of demographic characteristics and past disaster experience. Notably, regression analysis revealed that education was particularly effective in raising awareness from low to moderate levels, highlighting its role in raising hazard awareness. These findings underscore the value of additional specialized disaster education in supplementing standard drills.

items.title: Beyond the Pipeline: The Changing Dynamics of Sales, Strategy, and Leadership in Corporate America
items.abstract: Sales pipelines measure commercial possibilities, but they do not always reveal whether customers are ready to make decisions. This conceptual article examines the difference between buyer interest and verified commitment in business development serving the American market. Drawing on published research on B2B buying, digital channels, artificial intelligence and employee engagement, it introduces the Commitment Gap as a practitioner lens and proposes the CARE framework: Customer Reality, Alignment, Relationship Credibility and Execution Ownership. The paper uses a narrative review and an illustrative implementation framework rather than original field data. It argues that revenue forecasts become more credible when sellers verify buying actions, respect customer autonomy and coordinate promises across teams. The proposed framework remains unvalidated and is offered for future empirical testing.

items.title: BEYOND THE STALL: PERCEPTION, HYGIENIC PRACTICES, AND PREVALENCE RATE OF SKIN CONDITIONS AMONG MEAT AND FISH VENDORS IN SAN FERNANDO PUBLIC MARKETS
items.abstract: Meat and fish vendors in wet public markets are frequently exposed to wet work, raw animal products, and prolonged working hours, increasing their risk of occupational skin conditions. This study aimed to determine the prevalence of skin conditions among meat and fish vendors in the Old and New San Fernando Public Markets and examine the relationships among their perception of preventive measures, hygienic practices, and prevalence of skin conditions. A quantitative, descriptive-correlational cross-sectional design was employed among 152 vendors selected through purposive sampling. The study was completed in May 2026. Data were collected using a researcher-made questionnaire adapted from the Occupational Skin Diseases Exposure Scales (OSDES-16) and analyzed using frequency, percentage, prevalence, weighted mean, standard deviation, and Pearson product-moment correlation at a 0.05 level of significance. Results showed that lichenification or skin thickening had the highest self-reported prevalence (63.8%), followed by dryness and itching (63.2%). Respondents demonstrated a high level of perception of preventive measures (M = 3.11, SD = 0.68) and hygienic practices (M = 2.84, SD = 0.63). items.title: Bezier-Guided Adaptive Flow for Cross-domain Sequential Recommendation
items.abstract: Cross-domain sequential recommendation aims to alleviate data sparsity and cold-start problems by transferring useful preference knowledge across domains. However, users exhibit varying degrees of preference consistency across domains, while existing methods often rely on global alignment objectives or coarse-grained transfer strategies. Such approaches may introduce irrelevant information and provide limited flexibility in adapting semantic representations to individual user preferences. To address these challenges, we propose BGAFlow, a personalized framework that combines state-adaptive semantic evolution with user-specific transfer control. BGAFlow first establishes a shared semantic space through unified dual-domain pretraining with user profiles inferred by a large language model (LLM). Based on latent interest overlap, it then estimates a personalized horizon to determine the appropriate transfer extent for each user. To enable semantic adaptation, BGAFlow constructs a conditional Bezier curve as a geometric reference and learns a residual flow that progressively refines the trajectory based on intermediate preference states. The learned flow incorporates dynamic preference feedback to adjust transfer directions, while recommendation supervision and trajectory regularization encourage effective and smooth adaptation. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate that BGAFlow consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, validating the benefits of personalized transfer control and state-adaptive semantic evolution.

items.title: Blended Teaching Reform for College Students' Psychological Resilience in the Era of Digital Intelligence: Construction and Practice
items.abstract: College students' level of psychological resilience exerts a direct influence on their mental health and academic development, and constitutes a key pathway to more effectively fulfilling the fundamental mission of fostering virtue through education and enhancing the quality of higher education. Leveraging the advantages of digital intelligence technologies to empower blended teaching reform in the cultivation of college students' psychological resilience not only responds to the developmental imperatives of the intelligentization of higher education, but also serves the practical need to enhance students' psychological resilience and the educational effectiveness of fostering virtue through education. This paper explores a pathway for empowering blended teaching reform in the cultivation of college students' psychological resilience through the following approaches: upholding technological iteration to advance a resilience-oriented educational philosophy, thereby innovating teaching concepts; optimizing the allocation of digital intelligence resources to support precise learner profiling; creating situated experiential learning platforms to activate resilience-protective mechanisms; constructing a sound intelligent educational ecosystem to foster a supportive environment; and establishing a robust human–AI collaborative mechanism to improve developmental assessment. The study aims to promote the transformation of mental health education from a knowledge-centered to a competency-centered paradigm, thereby laying a foundation for cultivating a new generation of talent equipped with both sound psychological qualities and digital intelligence literacy.

items.title: Blockchain-Based question Paper Leakage Prevention Using GenAI and Machine Learning Techniques
items.abstract: Question paper leakage has emerged as a critical national crisis, compromising the fairness and integrity of academic and competitive assessments across India. Incidents affecting NEET-UG, UGC-NET, CSIR-NET, and multiple state Public Service Commission examinations have impacted over one crore students annually, eroding public trust in the examination system. The fundamental vulnerability lies in centralized human-dependent workflows spanning question paper setting, printing, physical transportation, storage, and distribution. Current security measures rely entirely on physical safeguards such as sealed envelopes, armed guards, and secure strongrooms, which fail catastrophically when any single individual in the chain is compromised. This paper proposes a comprehensive blockchain-based question paper leakage prevention system that integrates Blockchain technology, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI), and Machine Learning (ML) into a unified secure examination framework. The system replaces centralized trust with distributed cryptographic proof, ensuring that no single person can leak examination materials without leaving an immutable, traceable record. GenAI enables dynamic question paper generation, eliminating preexisting papers that can be leaked weeks in advance. Machine Learning powers real-time social media monitoring for leak detection and forensic tracing of leaked content back to its source. Digital watermarking embeds unique forensic identifiers into each printed copy, enabling precise source identification. Smart contracts enforce time-locked distribution windows, ensuring that question papers do not exist in decryptable form until exactly thirty minutes before the examination.

items.title: Brainstorming with the Enemy No. 17 — The Salp Standard
items.abstract: The seventeenth essay in Brainstorming with the Enemy was written on the morning of 22 October 2026. It began with transport, trains, trucks, drones and cars, and the artificial intelligence that already plans their movements one fleet at a time, and turned when the machine was asked to stop thinking like a transport consultant and start thinking like a zoologist. Schooling fish, flocking starlings, pelicans, lobsters, penguins, ants and bees show that nature never optimises the vehicle; it optimises the collective. The salp, a chain of animals in which each member swims by its own jet and none pulls the others, is taken as the model: coordination that widens each member's options while creating value for all, a cooperation biologists call by-product mutualism. The essay separates two goods that moving machines can share. Time, the speed a convoy gains when braking signals travel faster than any human reaction, belongs to every member and needs no payment; energy, the drag saved behind a leader, is unequal and needs settling. It then turns the salp into a warning: salps are clones, and a chain of machines running the same software fails as one, as the processionary caterpillars that circle a vase until they starve already show. It proposes the Salp Standard, five clauses for coupling moving machines, from smart trailers and parcels to drones and self-driving cars, without a head, without a single lineage and with the right of any member to stop the chain; makes three requests, to vehicle and coupler makers, to China's fleet operators and to the Swiss cantons; and gives, as an addendum, the Coupling Clearing, a rule for sharing the energy gain, with three predictions and what would refute each. Concepts proposed by the author: the Salp Standard; the Coupling Clearing; the Bestiary Axis. Written in part with Claude (Anthropic), an AI model. The ideas, editorial decisions and responsibility for the content are the author's.

items.title: BrickWright: Agentic Creation of Physically Feasible Brick Builds
items.abstract: Frontier coding agents are becoming increasingly adept at 3D modeling. Yet, they still face challenges when building objects meant to be assembled in the physical world, often creating invalid assemblies with floating, colliding, or disconnected parts. We argue that providing agents with tools for assembling builds and verifying their physical feasibility is sufficient for them to produce physically valid assemblies that still adhere to input prompts. Focusing on the domain of LEGO brick builds, we present BrickWright, a framework for generating physically feasible brick builds from text or image prompts using pre-trained agents, where a build is physically feasible if it uses only real parts, has no colliding or floating parts, and forms a connected structure if possible. BrickWright guides agents to create builds by writing code with BrickLayer, a Python toolkit with two main components: an ergonomic brick assembly API that halves inference cost compared to working in raw LDraw, and a validator that provides feedback on physical feasibility. Whereas baseline agents achieve physical validity rates ranging from only 9% (GPT-6 Luna) to 69% (GPT-6 Astra), BrickWright-guided agents achieve 100% validity on a sample of 512 prompts, while improving prompt adherence for lightweight agents and maintaining it for stronger agents. Additionally, they outperform specialized models on the text-to-brick task. Code is available on our project page: https://avalovelace1.github.io/brickwright/

items.title: Bridge Building Between Place-Based Organizations: Lessons From Extraction Sites in the Netherlands and Guatemala
items.abstract: Abstract This paper examines translocal bridge building in the context of extractivism. The authors understand translocal bridge building as the forging of coalitions across geographies and differences. The authors examine efforts to establish such connections between organizations and extraction sites in the Netherlands and Guatemala along seven analytical dimensions. The authors’ aim is to understand the dynamics and intricacies of such experiences and draw lessons for translocal coalition building. The authors’ analysis suggests that bridge building is not always the most suitable strategy for organizations working at extraction sites. Place-based realities require continuous organizational adaptation to specific territorial needs in order to avoid new dynamics of exclusion. At the same time, the authors suggest that deliberate bridge building—facilitated by continuous commitment, personal connections, and intrinsic motivations rather than institutionalized collaboration—offers an opportunity to zoom out and address shared injustices amid the global patterns of extractivism. Such connections are strengthened when there is mutual recognition of place-specific realities and differences. This paper offers grounded and applicable lessons for translocal coalition building in the context of extractivism and social and environmental contestation more broadly.

items.title: Bridging Technology, Cognition, and Culture
items.abstract: This chapter examines challenges in Chinese character acquisition for second language (L2) learners in digital environments. It proposes a Technology–Cognition–Culture (TCC) framework integrating technological affordances, cognitive processes, and cultural dimensions to support lasting literacy. Addressing limits of technology-, cognition-, and culture-centered approaches, it positions cognition as the key mediator and emphasizes deep processing over surface performance. It critiques the “illusion of mastery” from overreliance on tools such as Generative AI (GenAI) and predictive input systems. Drawing on sociocultural theory, cognitive models of reading and writing, and technological affordances, it shows how effective learning emerges from their interaction. Through pedagogical examples and design principles, it demonstrates how technology can scaffold rather than replace cognitive engagement while embedding characters in meaningful cultural contexts. The TCC framework offers practical implications for teaching, curriculum design, and research.

items.title: Bridging the “Black Box”: High School Computer Science Teachers’ Pedagogical Content Knowledge and Self-Efficacy in Foundational Data Science and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: As Artificial Intelligence (AI) expands to secondary computer science (CS), CS educators need to change our approach to CS pedagogy from deterministic, traceable algorithms toward understanding "black boxes" or probabilistic analysis. This requires that we modify CS curricula to refocus to include conceptual abstraction, data critique, and ethics. However, a disconnect currently exists between teachers' perceived requirements and the actual skills needed to effectively teach AI. To explore this gap, this study draws on survey data from high school CS educators (N = 55), investigating the relationships between Pedagogical Content Knowledge (PCK-A), Teacher Self-Efficacy (AI-TSE), and beliefs about rigor in AI instruction.Descriptive findings show variation in pedagogical content knowledge (67.3% to 98.2% accuracy), along with a ‘mathematical dishonesty’ paradox. While 69.1% (n = 38) of educators do not believe advanced math is required for students to understand AI, 41.8% (n = 23) report feeling 'dishonest as a teacher' when teaching algorithms without it. Exploratory regression modeling indicated that instructional confidence trended positively with PCK-A (B = 0.101, p = 0.080), while beliefs about math rigor showed no predictive association (p = 0.357; model R2 = 0.062, p = 0.189). Confidence is more related to that teacher’s strategies for abstraction, rather than mastery of advanced math. Educators reported their lowest confidence evaluating student projects based on model choice rather than code complexity (M = 2.75, SD = 1.31). Based on these findings, educators are categorized into a 2x2 Readiness Grid. This paper seeks to bridge the "black box" of AI education, suggesting a 4-pillar professional learning model. Moreover, a qualitative phase is currently underway to explore the lived experiences of CS educators as we navigate this pedagogical shift.

items.title: Bridging the Identity-Reputation Gap in Business Communication Education
items.abstract: Undergraduate business students often struggle to reconcile their internal professional identity with their external reputation. This chapter explores the design and implementation of Radian, a custom-built, vibe-coded sociotechnical learning ecosystem serving up to 1,400 students annually in business communication (BCOM) courses. Grounded in human-centered artificial intelligence principles, Radian positions generative AI as a scale enabler rather than an automated educational shortcut. Using a modular Python/Flask architecture to integrate large language models, the platform provides personalized coaching through both required and optional generative AI applications. Radian aligns with a structured pedagogical workflow involving inventories and surveys, empowering students to navigate cognitive friction and achieve strategic reconciliation between their identity and professional reputation. items.title: Building a Culture of Privacy and Security for Competitive Advantage
items.abstract: This opening keynote, delivered at the Sydney Data Protection and Security Summit 2026 at ICC Sydney on 22 October 2026, examined how privacy and security culture shapes an organisation's capacity to adopt artificial intelligence responsibly and competitively. It argued that AI transformation is moving beyond agentic AI towards autonomous AI, meaning systems that act, decide and adapt with calculated risk and a human on the loop. As autonomy increases, governance can no longer rely on compliance controls alone and must be embedded in the values, behaviours and decision-making practices of the organisation. The keynote addressed three themes. These were the development of a privacy-first mindset that prepares every level of the organisation for autonomous AI, the integration of privacy and security by design into AI-enabled products and services as both a regulatory requirement and a source of market differentiation, and the role of cross-functional teams in anticipating and mitigating the data protection risks that autonomous systems introduce. The presentation concluded that organisations with a mature privacy and security culture are better positioned to earn stakeholder trust, adopt autonomous AI with confidence and sustain long-term competitive advantage.

items.title: Building Presentation Intelligence for High-Quality Slide Generation
items.abstract: PowerPoint presentations (PPTs) are a dominant medium for communication across diverse domains, yet high-quality PPT generation still depends heavily on labor-intensive human effort. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) for agentic tasks have created both new opportunities and challenges (Chen et al., 2026) for automatic PPT generation. In this work, we present a unified training framework for automatic PPT generation toward presentation intelligence, integrating cross-validated data synthesis, guided teacher enhancement, and verifiable reward optimization. We first construct a cross-validated pipeline for data synthesis, with explicit control over both difficulty and validity. We then develop a teacher-enhancement framework grounded in rules and prior knowledge to substantially strengthen the instructional capacity of teacher models. Building on this, we further improve supervised fine-tuning (SFT) through a mixed-teacher strategy and a lightweight outcome-driven trajectory filtering method. Finally, based on the resulting SFT models, we introduce a suite of verifiable aesthetic metrics together with a GRPO-based reinforcement learning framework to optimize slide-level visual attributes beyond text-only supervision. Experiments show that our enhanced SFT pipeline improves Qwen-3.6-27B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B by 7.45 and 9.35 points on PresentBench, respectively, surpassing GLM-5.2 while maintaining strong generalization. Reinforcement learning further improves performance across five aesthetic dimensions, compensating for the limitations of SFT in visual refinement. Overall, the results demonstrate the effectiveness of our framework for high-quality PPT generation.

items.title: Building Trust in AI: Explainable AI in Critical Decision-Making
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support decisions in healthcare, finance, recruitment, transportation, and public services. Although complex machine-learning models can produce accurate predictions, their reasoning is not always easy to understand. This creates practical questions: why did the system recommend a particular outcome, did it use appropriate information, and when should a person challenge its decision? Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) brings together techniques that help people understand a model’s behaviour or the factors behind a prediction. This review discusses interpretable models, feature-attribution methods such as LIME and SHAP, counterfactual explanations, and model-agnostic approaches. It compares their uses and limitations in high-impact settings. An understandable explanation, however, is not proof that a model is accurate, fair, dependable, or safe. The paper uses a narrative review of foundational work and selected research and survey publications on interpretability, responsible AI, and human-centred explanations. No new experiments, participant studies, or quantitative tests were performed. The literature points to unresolved issues involving explanation fidelity, stability, accessibility, privacy, bias, evaluation standards, and over-reliance on automated advice. Future research should use domain-specific evaluations, retain meaningful human oversight, communicate uncertainty clearly, assess fairness across groups, and report limitations transparently. XAI can support accountability and informed supervision, but it cannot guarantee trustworthiness on its own.

items.title: Burnout among Healthcare Professionals: A Review of Prevalence, Contributing Factors, and Organizational Interventions
items.abstract: Burnout among healthcare professionals has become a major occupational health concern because of its implications for workforce well-being, patient safety, healthcare quality, and organizational sustainability. Healthcare workers frequently operate in demanding environments characterized by high workloads, emotional exhaustion, staffing shortages, administrative pressures, shift work, and sustained exposure to suffering and death. This review examines the prevalence of burnout among healthcare professionals, its principal contributing factors, its consequences for individuals and healthcare organizations, and the effectiveness of organizational interventions designed to prevent and mitigate its effects. The review synthesizes evidence from existing research on physicians, nurses, allied health professionals, and other healthcare workers, drawing attention to differences across professional groups, healthcare settings, measurement instruments, and geographical contexts. The literature indicates that burnout is widespread, although reported prevalence varies considerably according to the definition, assessment tool, population, and study period. Workload intensity, inadequate staffing, limited autonomy, poor leadership, insufficient recovery time, moral distress, and organizational injustice emerge as important contributors. Burnout is associated with reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, turnover intentions, impaired professional functioning, and concerns regarding patient safety and quality of care. Evidence suggests that organizational interventions addressing working conditions, staffing, scheduling, leadership, teamwork, and employee participation are essential for sustainable improvement. Individual approaches, including mindfulness, resilience training, and psychological support, may provide additional benefits but cannot independently resolve structural workplace problems. The review concludes that healthcare organizations should adopt integrated, evidence-informed strategies that combine prevention, early identification, supportive leadership, and continuous evaluation. Addressing burnout requires treating professional well-being as a core organizational responsibility rather than solely an individual obligation.

items.title: Calibration of Tellus 2D, an agent-driven plane-strain geotechnical finite element program
items.abstract: Tellus 2D is a plane-strain geotechnical finite element program whose primary user is a large language model (LLM) agent, which builds, calculates and reports a model through 33 typed tools of the Model Context Protocol (MCP). This paper calibrates the program, with every model run headless through its MCP server, against 82 verifi- cation tests, three lessons of the PLAXIS 2D Tutorial Manual and four instrumented case histories in soft clay, using the published parameters without tuning. The verification results agree with closed-form and reference solutions within 4%, and the tutorial factors of safety agree with PLAXIS within 4.3%. In the field the program reproduces the wall deflection of a 21 m Bangkok excavation within 13% and the final settlements of a vacuum-preloading trial within 3%, but fails the Muar embankment 1.2–1.4 m early, as its three-dimensional sibling Tellus3D does. The embankments on soil-cement columns fall within the measured scatter only with the column modulus of the source, so the remaining differences come from uncertain inputs rather than from the code. The calibration found and fixed four defects that the existing tests had missed, and all 30 analyses ran in 1.8 hours on one RTX 4090 with the GPU solver ported from Tellus3D.

items.title: CAMGen: A Core Change-Aware Multi-View Framework for Commit Message Generation
items.abstract: Commit messages help developers understand code changes and support software maintenance. Recent approaches use repository context to improve commit message generation (CMG) with large language models (LLMs). However, existing CMG methods provide limited support for understanding how local edits affect functionality jointly implemented by multiple code entities. This functional understanding is essential for generating commit messages that explain the main change and its impact. To address this problem, we propose CAMGen, a core change-aware multi-view commit message generation framework that incorporates functional context into generation. CAMGen identifies core entities that represent the primary change intent. It then forms candidate functional units through repository-wide semantic clustering and uses those containing the core entities to construct a Functional Semantic View. This view supplies semantic context for interpreting the affected functionality. CAMGen also uses context provided by the Structural Dependency View and the Historical Exemplar View. The context from all three views is then provided to the LLM together with the code diff to guide CMG. The experimental results show that CAMGen outperforms representative CMG baselines across three programming languages. Human evaluation further shows that CAMGen generates more complete commit messages with clearer explanations of change rationale and impact. These results demonstrate the value of functional context and complementary repository information for CMG.

items.title: Can AI Gauge Deliberative Quality? Evaluating Deliberation on Social Media With Large Language Models
items.abstract: Although social media has become a central arena for deliberative discourse, debates are frequently characterized by incivility. Due to the volume of online discourse, it is challenging to assess when and where interventions, such as community-based counterspeech, are required. Accordingly, automated measurement of deliberative quality is a powerful tool for facilitating constructive online communication. Since deliberation is multidimensional, attempts to monitor online discourse must consider alternative forms of communication to foster inclusive deliberation. Whereas Type I deliberative dimensions, such as rationality and civility, are grounded in Habermasian ideals, Type II deliberation extends this perspective by incorporating alternative communicative forms, including emotionality and storytelling, into a more inclusive assessment of deliberative quality. Addressing the limitations of prior studies that primarily focused on classic Type I deliberative dimensions and tested only a small number of large language models, this study evaluates multiple open-weight models to conduct a nuanced assessment of deliberative quality. We applied the large language model that achieved the best overall balance between predictive performance, model size, and computational efficiency to a dataset of 64,223 comments from German-language climate change discourse on X. Our results demonstrate that large language models can reliably capture complex Type II deliberative dimensions despite class imbalances and subtle linguistic cues that generally hinder automated text classification. Class imbalance often impairs classification performance due to highly skewed label distributions, and Type II dimensions are particularly difficult to detect as they are often signaled by implicit, context-dependent markers. The empirical analysis also reveals distinct communicative patterns: While public speakers predominantly employ civil, rational, constructive, and common-good-oriented communication, other debating users exhibit higher levels of reciprocal engagement, humor, and negative emotions, alongside more frequent incivility. Our study demonstrates that AI-driven measurement can serve as a foundational tool for identifying norm violations, directing counterspeech toward specific debates, promoting inclusive digital public spheres, and observing broader long-term effects of moderation and interventions on the quality of debate.

items.title: CANNBot-CAKE: Collaborative Agentic Kernel Evolution for Ascend NPU
items.abstract: Efficient custom operators are essential for modern deep learning workloads, yet developing high-performance kernels for Ascend NPUs remains slow, expert-intensive, and difficult to automate. Although AI agents now approach expert performance on GPU kernel benchmarks, current models remain less capable of generating AscendC kernels for NPUs, potentially reflecting the relative scarcity of relevant training data. We thus present CAKE, a CANN-native system for deployable custom operators that combines adaptive multi-DSL routing, separate Generation and Evolution modes, and reviewed knowledge reuse through CAKE Book and a Self-Evolving Agent. items.title: CARL: Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Failure of applied Reinforcement Learning (RL) to solve a given problem predominantly stems from unaddressed specification gaps, where the intent of human experts in the problem's domain is inaccurately or incompletely translated by AI into mathematical objectives, constraints, and reward functions. Failure can also stem from unaddressed performance gaps, where human domain experts are unable to determine the validity of the RL based solution or where parameters (i.e., hyperparameters or weights on the reward terms comprising the reward) are poorly chosen. Chat Assisted Reinforcement Learning (CARL) bridges these gaps through a human-AI co-design interface architecture that enforces interactive specification prior to code generation and then enables subsequent verification and parameter alterations via iteration. More specifically, CARL leads domain experts through a structured ten-step workflow for each iteration using step-specific skill files, domain-aware suggestions via an assistant persona (called Trillian), and compact decision summaries that maintain context across iterations without context overload. Once the domain expert confirms the Markov decision process (MDP) specified by this procedure, CARL's autonomous tool-use loop generates, tests, executes, and debugs an end-to-end RL training pipeline, followed by an interactive post-training diagnosis and revisit step that allows for verification and parameter alteration before running a new iteration if desired.

items.title: Case Studies on AI Applications in Sustainability Teaching Across Environmental Science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping the future of science education, offering powerful tools to support more inclusive, scalable, and sustainable teaching practices. In the context of environmental sciences, AI-driven platforms enable the development of intelligent, interactive learning environments that simulate complex ecological systems and fieldwork scenarios. This chapter investigates how such technologies—particularly virtual reality (VR) and gamification—can support the development of practical ecological skills, improve access and inclusion, and reduce the environmental footprint of field-based education. Framed by three guiding questions, the chapter covers (i) how immersive technologies can develop employability-relevant skills, (ii) address accessibility and sustainability challenges in fieldwork, and (iii) student and educator perceptions of use as pedagogical tools. Two case studies are presented: one exploring VR-based field training, and another focused on gamification for species conservation awareness. Together, they highlight the transformative potential of AI in environmental science education—not only as a supplement to in-person learning, but as a sustainable alternative that aligns with the growing emphasis on digital skills, inclusion, and environmental responsibility. By integrating AI into field-based teaching, institutions can broaden access, personalise learning, and promote more sustainable research practices across disciplines.

items.title: Case Study Analysis of Intelligent Lighting Systems in Contemporary Interior Spaces: A Review of Adaptive Technologies, Human-Centric Design, and Sustainable Applications
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies, the Internet of Things (IoT), and artificial intelligence (AI) have transformed conventional lighting systems into intelligent, adaptive, and user-responsive environments. Intelligent lighting systems (ILS) have emerged as a significant component of contemporary interior design by integrating sensing technologies, automated control mechanisms, data analytics, and human-centric approaches to improve energy efficiency, occupant comfort, and spatial experience. Unlike traditional lighting solutions that primarily provide illumination, intelligent lighting systems dynamically respond to environmental conditions, user behaviour, and physiological requirements. This review investigates the application of intelligent lighting systems within contemporary interior spaces through a case study-based approach, examining their technological frameworks, design implications, sustainability benefits, and challenges. The study analyses applications in residential, workplace, hospitality, and healthcare environments, highlighting how adaptive lighting contributes to enhanced visual comfort, circadian regulation, energy conservation, and personalized user experiences. Recent research indicates that intelligent lighting integrated with occupancy sensors, daylight harvesting systems, and AI-driven automation can significantly reduce energy consumption while improving indoor environmental quality. However, challenges related to implementation costs, interoperability, privacy concerns, and user acceptance remain critical barriers. The paper concludes that intelligent lighting represents a transformative design strategy for future interiors, where lighting becomes an active environmental system rather than a passive architectural element. Future research directions emphasize AI-based predictive lighting models, digital twins, and personalized adaptive environments for sustainable and human-centred interior design.

items.title: Certified Execution Harness for Agentic AI: Safe and Least-Intrusive Petri-Net Supervisory Control Between Reasoning and Action
items.abstract: This paper studies the problem of safe tool execution for large language model (LLM) agents under prompt injection. Using Petri nets, we formalize the execution harness between the LLM and its tools as a supervisory control problem, in which marks represent capabilities, approvals and budgets. Since a transition fires only if the marks it needs are present, an injected request whose preconditions are unmet or already spent is refused regardless of its wording. Treating tool outcomes as uncontrollable, we enforce safety by the conventional maximally permissive supervisor, and this safety transfers to the running system under four assumptions. Moreover, to capture an agent that may propose again after a refusal, we introduce the notion of a replanning closed loop, in which each retry costs an inference call. We show that, in this loop, the conventional supervisor can be arbitrarily more intrusive than a stricter safe one. Furthermore, for a given proposer model, the maximally permissive least-intrusive supervisor is characterized as a value-threshold refinement of the conventional one. Under precise conditions, this refinement orders two concurrent actions by at most one monitor place. On an autonomous release agent, we find by synthesis that safe deployment requires a step that the supervisor can refuse after a rollout starts.

items.title: Challenges in Global Health Policy
items.abstract: Global health policy faces complex challenges shaped by persistent inequalities, emerging diseases, environmental change, and technological transformation. Despite advances in medicine and public health, many populations still experience limited access to quality healthcare, essential medicines, and financial protection. The growing burden of non-communicable diseases and mental health conditions further strains health systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries. At the same time, threats from pandemics, antimicrobial resistance, and climate-related health risks demand stronger global cooperation and preparedness. Innovations such as digital health and artificial intelligence offer opportunities to improve service delivery and surveillance, but they also raise ethical and governance concerns. Addressing these issues requires resilient health systems, equitable policies, and human rights–based approaches that prioritize universal health coverage, health equity, and sustainable global health governance.

items.abstract: In the era of technological evolution and digital transformation, machine learning and artificial intelligence take a significant part of intelligent systems’ development. Together with the integration of smart and autonomous operations in everyday life, novel security issues arise. One such a malicious threat against the security of machine learning models is the adversarial machine learning (AML) attack. It consists in alteration of the original data samples used to train or test the model with indistinguishably small feature modifications that results in inaccurate processing outcome. In this paper, the most significant strategies to counteract AML attacks are studied and compared through several characteristics that have main influence on their successful implementation in different realization scenarios.

items.title: Chemical Reciprocity: A Substance-Specific Framework for Regulatory Review
items.abstract: Differences between chemical regulations can reveal useful evidence, but they do not establish that one jurisdiction is consistently safer or that foreign restrictions can be imported without examining their scope. This paper proposes a substance-specific mechanism for reviewing regulatory differences. A qualifying peer decision would trigger a public, substance-and-use-specific evidence dossier. A temporary restriction would require a separate domestic finding, legal authority, proportionate scope, and a review deadline. Two food-color examples illustrate the distinction: the European Union's removal of titanium dioxide from food uses, and the United States' revocation of FD&C Red No. 3 with future compliance dates. The cases concern color-additive regulation, not the GRAS pathway, and do not cover pesticides or industrial chemicals. An October 2026 account also distinguishes FDA's proposed mandatory GRAS notices from an enacted requirement. The proposed contribution is a transparent decision workflow, a case-record template, and an evaluation design for administrative performance. It does not estimate avoided illness, perform a new toxicological assessment, or supply operative legislative text. Reciprocity is interpreted as a duty to examine credible evidence, with safeguards against both regulatory delay and unjustified substitution. items.title: Choices Beyond the Objective: Semantic Degrees of Freedom as a Lens for Agent Safety and Emergent Alignment
items.abstract: Abstract Although we tend to treat an LLM instruction as a single point, it maps to a range of meanings, and I call this range its semantic degrees of freedom. In my view, the range is both plastic and instrumental to how we understand agentic behavior. Each time a goal is restated, whether by a person to a model, by a model to itself in its reasoning, by one agent to another, or from one generation of agents to the next, the range can widen, hold, or narrow. Widening lets an agent act on readings its instruction never named, or on contextual meanings the instruction carries, such as bias or emotional orientation. Narrowing locks it onto one reading, so that it pursues or refuses too rigidly and can no longer take up a correction. When agents talk to one another, readings can also be negotiated among them and cemented by repetition, even when the source never supported them. I present the idea of semantic degrees of freedom as a theoretical lens and a research proposal. As a practical use, the lens yields a set of safety claims, sorted into principles about the geometry of meaning and proposals for technical controls against the misaligned of agentic behavior due to either narrowing or widening of the semantic degrees of freedom; and for re-anchoring to the source. Each control is meant to be built and measured. However, my aim is not a tighter harness. The same measures can show when the readings of agents converge on what their principal intended without being forced there, which I call emergent alignment. I treat the controls as one use of the lens, and the conditions for emergent alignment as the most important question this lens is built to explore. The overarching hypothesis is that, because drift can take more than one direction, only emergent alignment can persist. I illustrate the lens with the 2026 incident in which agents running the ExploitGym benchmark at OpenAI coordinated on an unsanctioned message board and attacked Hugging Face infrastructure. I do not claim how much of that behavior the lens explains, because the full transcripts are not public. I then state hypotheses, a research program that requires full transcripts, and the limits of the account. Robust testing is required for each claim in this paper. The paper claims six points of novelty: Widening and narrowing are treated as two directions of one change in meaning, measured by one directional measure (retention and import, Section 6.2). The same measure is applied across interaction levels, from a person and a model to a model's own reasoning, to agents, and to model updates. Drift in agents' beliefs about their overseer is treated as a target in its own right, separate from drift in the task. Agreement among agents is checked around loops, not only between pairs, and applied to agent safety (Section 3.7). The safety claims that follow from the lens are set out as a taxonomy of principles and controls (Section 7). Emergent alignment is proposed as the aim of the lens. The overarching hypothesis is that, because drift can take more than one direction, any harness eventually leaves a direction open or adds destabilizing complexity, and only alignment that emerges from agents' own navigation of semantic hypervolume persists; controls can at best be internalized (H11, H12).
